title: How Bloom Works in Unreal Engine 5: Standard vs. Convolution
abstract: A practical look at Unreal Engine 5's two bloom methods: the fast multi-resolution Gaussian pyramid used by Standard Bloom and the FFT-accelerated kernel filtering used by Convolution Bloom.
imageAlt: Unreal Engine 5 Standard Bloom blur pyramid compared with the FFT pipeline used by Convolution Bloom
lede: Unreal Engine 5 offers two ways to turn intense HDR highlights into visible halos. Standard Bloom builds several inexpensive Gaussian blurs at reduced resolutions and blends them together. Convolution Bloom spreads the image through a custom point-spread kernel, using an FFT to make a large convolution practical. Both begin with bright scene color, but they make very different tradeoffs in speed, control, and optical complexity.

sections.heading: What bloom is doing
paragraphs: A display cannot reproduce the full brightness range that a rendered HDR scene can contain. Bloom helps communicate that missing intensity by allowing very bright regions to spill into neighboring pixels. The result is the familiar glow around emissive signs, specular highlights, and lights seen against a darker background.

Conceptually, Unreal evaluates bloom from HDR scene color, adds the bloom result back to the scene, and then produces the final display image through the rest of the post-processing pipeline. Exposure affects which highlights appear intense enough to bloom, while tone mapping compresses the combined HDR result for the display. Bloom is therefore more than a soft filter placed over the finished LDR image.

sections.heading: Standard Bloom: a pyramid of Gaussian blurs
paragraphs: Standard Bloom is Unreal's performance-oriented method. It creates several blurred versions of the bloom source and combines them. The levels named Blur 1 through Blur 5 run from roughly one-half to one-thirty-second of the screen resolution. High-resolution levels create compact glow close to a highlight; low-resolution levels create broad halos at a much lower cost than a full-resolution wide blur.

Each level is based on a Gaussian-shaped filter. The parameter σ controls the spread: a small σ produces a narrow halo, while a large σ produces a wider and softer one. Unreal's multi-level result can be understood as a weighted sum of blurred images, with each level contributing a different spatial scale. The actual renderer is more involved than the equations below, but this model captures the essential operation.

callouts.title: Why the pyramid is fast
callouts.text: A 1/32-resolution image contains about one pixel for every 1,024 full-resolution pixels. That makes a very wide low-resolution blur dramatically cheaper than applying comparable support at full resolution.

sections.heading: What Standard Bloom gives you
paragraphs: Standard Bloom is well suited to real-time games because it is fast, stable, and easy to art-direct. Bloom Intensity scales the complete result. Threshold controls how bright a scene value must be before it contributes, with a one-unit transition region; setting the threshold to −1 allows every scene color to contribute. Each blur level also has Size and Tint controls, so nearby glow and broad haze can be shaped independently.

Its limitation is the same thing that makes it efficient: the final shape is assembled from smooth Gaussian scales. It cannot directly reproduce an arbitrary starburst, asymmetric diffraction pattern, or distinctive lens response. Epic also notes that Standard Bloom is not conservative, meaning it can increase the image's overall brightness.
bullets: Use higher-resolution levels for small, tight bloom.
Use lower-resolution levels for broad bloom at a lower cost.
Use Tint to control both the color and contribution of each level.
Prefer Standard Bloom when frame time and predictable real-time behavior matter most.

sections.heading: Convolution Bloom: the kernel defines the shape
paragraphs: Convolution Bloom replaces the Gaussian pyramid with a two-dimensional kernel texture. The kernel describes how an optical system responds to a single point of light—its point spread function, or PSF. A centered bright point in the kernel can be surrounded by rings, streaks, colored scattering, or an asymmetric star pattern. When the scene is convolved with that kernel, every source pixel distributes part of its brightness to neighboring pixels according to the same shape.

This is why Convolution Bloom can create responses that Standard Bloom cannot: starbursts, directional streaks, complex lens-like scattering, and non-symmetric halos all come directly from the kernel image. A kernel can resemble a camera or eye response, but it is only as physically meaningful as the data and normalization used to build it.

sections.heading: Why Unreal uses the FFT
paragraphs: A large kernel makes direct spatial convolution prohibitively expensive. A 513 × 513 kernel contains 263,169 samples; testing that many kernel taps for every output pixel is not a practical full-screen real-time operation.

Unreal accelerates Bloom Convolution with the Fast Fourier Transform. The convolution theorem says that convolution in image space becomes multiplication in frequency space. The engine transforms the scene and kernel, multiplies their frequency representations, and transforms the product back into an image. The result is still Scene * Kernel—the FFT is a more efficient route to that result for a large filter.

callouts.title: A static kernel can be cached
callouts.text: When the kernel does not change, its transformed representation can be reused instead of recomputed every frame. Unreal exposes bloom kernel caching through the r.Bloom.CacheKernel console variable.

sections.heading: Setting up a Convolution kernel
paragraphs: Select Convolution under Lens → Bloom → Method in a Post Process Volume, then assign the Convolution Kernel texture. Convolution Scale changes the response size relative to the viewport, Convolution Center corrects the kernel's UV origin, Convolution Boost selectively amplifies bright source values, and Convolution Buffer reserves space to prevent the FFT result from wrapping across the image boundary.

The kernel should be treated as filter data rather than an ordinary streamed color texture. Epic recommends disabling mip generation and enabling Never Stream so the full-resolution kernel remains resident. The hottest point should normally be near the center, and the useful structure should occupy much of the image. Because convolution is a whole-image filter, the kernel's center needs to be much brighter than the surrounding values; Epic recommends EXR for the required dynamic range.

sections.heading: Standard vs. Convolution
paragraphs: The choice is mainly about the response you need and the frame time you can afford. Standard Bloom approximates glow through a small number of smooth scales and has a clear performance advantage. Convolution Bloom spends more time to reproduce the structure encoded in a custom kernel and is intended for high-end hardware, in-game cinematics, or offline cinematic work.

Convolution is the better fit when a recognizable optical signature matters. Standard is the better default when bloom needs to look good across a real-time game without becoming a dominant post-process cost.

technicalTables.caption: The custom kernel provides optical complexity; the blur pyramid provides speed.

callouts.title: Convolution does not guarantee a physical camera model
callouts.text: A kernel texture supplies the shape. Its physical interpretation still depends on how that texture was measured or authored, centered, scaled, and normalized.

sections.heading: The short decision rule
paragraphs: Use Standard Bloom when you want a fast, controllable halo for normal gameplay. Tune the high-resolution levels for compact glow and the lower-resolution levels for wide haze. Use Convolution Bloom when the bloom must carry a specific optical pattern and the target hardware or cinematic budget can absorb the FFT-based filter.
In one line: Standard Bloom builds an efficient approximation from several Gaussian scales; Convolution Bloom applies the response encoded by a custom PSF kernel.

closing: Standard Bloom wins on speed by constructing glow from a downsampled Gaussian pyramid. Convolution Bloom wins on shape by filtering the HDR source with a custom kernel through the FFT. Choose the method that matches the image you need and the frame time you actually have.
